Boundary controllability of two coupled wave equations with space-time first-order coupling in 1−D1-D

Affiliation: Farid Ammar Khodja and Affiliation: Yacine Mokhtari
Abstract

This paper is devoted to study exact controllability of two one-dimensional coupled wave equations with first-order coupling terms with coefficients depending on space and time. We give a necessary and sufficient condition for both exact controllability in high frequency in the general case and the unique continuation in the cascade case.

1 Introduction

We are interested in the boundary controllability of the following system of two strongly coupled 1−D1-D wave equations

{yt​t=yx​x+M⁡((a​y)t+(b​y)x),inQT:=(0,T)×(0,1),y(t,0)=Bu(t), y(t,1)=0, in(0,T), y(0,x)=y0(x), yt(0,x)=y1(x), in(0,1), \left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}y_{tt}=y_{xx}+M(\left(ay\right)_{t}+\left(by\right)_{x}),&\mathrm{in}&Q_{T}:=(0,T)\times(0,1),\\ y(t,0)=Bu(t),\text{ }y(t,1)=0,\text{ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ }&\mathrm{in}&(0,T),\text{ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ }\\ y(0,x)=y_{0}(x),\text{ }y_{t}(0,x)=y_{1}(x),\text{ \ \ }&\mathrm{in}&(0,1),\text{ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ }\end{array}\right. (1)

where y=(y1,y2)ty=(y_{1},y_{2})^{t} is a vector function and

M=(mi​j)1≤i,j≤2∈ℒ(ℝ2), B=(b1,b2)t∈ℝ2, a,b∈C1(QT¯;ℝ),M=(m_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq 2}\in\mathcal{L}\left(\mathbb{R}^{2}\right),\text{ }B=(b_{1},b_{2})^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{2},\text{ }a,b\in C^{1}(\overline{Q_{T}};\mathbb{R}), (2)

and uu a is scalar control function acting at x=0x=0.

This work is motivated by some previous papers. One of them is the result of Zhang [27]: a single wave equation in any space dimension with lower order terms is proved to be exactly controllable by a control acting on part of the boundary under a suitable geometric condition and independently from the lower terms. The author extended earlier Carleman inequalities proved by Fursikov-Imanuvilov [18] for the wave equation without these lower order terms.

The same issue arises for systems of nn (≥2)(\geq 2) coupled wave equations with boundary or distributed controls. In [1], Alabau-Boussouira studied the controllability of 22-coupled wave equations with zero order coupling operator with constant coefficients. Later, this result has been generalized by Alabau-Boussouira and Léautaud in [2], [3], for coupling coefficients depending on the space variable under the geometric control condition introduced in [10]. In these works, one of the coupling coefficients is supposed to be small.

Dehman, Le Rousseau and Léautaud [15] studied distributed controllability of 22-coupled wave equations on a Riemannian manifold without boundary (periodic boundary conditions in the 1−D1-D case) with a particular zero order coupling operator of cascade type. They proved that exact controllability holds provided that the Geometric Control Condition is satisfied. Further, they gave a characterization of the minimal time of control. An abstract result on the exact controllability of cascade systems is due to Alabau-Boussouira [4] (abstract setting with application to various coupled second order PDEs). In all these cited works, it has been assumed that the coupling functions are of constant sign.

A boundary controllability result has been established without the sign or the smallness conditions by Bennour et al. [11] for 22-coupled wave equations in 1−D1-D with cascade type coupling through velocity.

Concerning the constant case, Avdonin and De Tereza gave a complete answer for the exact boundary controllability issue for 22-coupled wave equations by zero order operator in 1−D1-D. The same authors came back in [9] and generalized their result to nn (≥2)(\geq 2) coupled wave equations in 1−D1-D but always with constant coupling coefficients under a Kalman rank condition. The same condition appears for distributed controllability of nn (≥2)(\geq 2)-coupled multidimensional wave equations with zero order coupling matrix with constant coefficients. It has been proved by Liard and Lissy in [20] that it is necessary and sufficient for the exact controllability in more regular energy space. An extension of this result can be found in Duprez and Olive [16] for cascade systems with zero order coupling operator whose coefficients depend on the space variable. However, boundary controllability has not been treated yet.

Recently, in [13], Cui et al. studied distributed controllability of nn (≥2)(\geq 2)-coupled wave equations with zero and first-order coupling operator whose coefficients depend on both space and time variables on a compact Riemannian manifold without boundary (periodic boundary conditions in the 1-D case). It has been shown that the exact controllability issue can be reduced to the controllability of a finite dimensional system along the associated Hamiltonian flow. The authors also gave a unique continuation results in the autonomous case under classical support and sign assumptions. The same idea appears in [5] by Alabau-Boussouira et al. where distributed controllability of 1−D1-D first-order system with periodic boundary conditions is considered. The authors proved that exact controllability is reduced to the controllability of parameterized non-autonomous finite dimensional system. We would also like to mention the recent paper by Coron and Nguyen [14] where they proved exact boundary controllability result for a hyperbolic system with space-time zero order term in 1−D.1-D. We emphasize that in this work the control matrix is invertible (the control acts on all the components with negative speeds).

In light of all of the cited works, we can see that the main issue that has to be solved is to figure out the optimal assumptions the coupling coefficients (or operators) of such systems must satisfy so that exact or approximate controllability hold with less number of controls.

In this article, and by using the characteristics method and a perturbation argument introduced in the pioneer work of Russell [25], we give a necessary and sufficient condition for the boundary exact controllability of System (1) in high frequency for a general matrix MM. We shall also propose a criterion for the unique continuation property in the cascade case. Actually, we will prove that the unique continuation property is equivalent to solving a system a 22-coupled Fredholm integral equations of the third kind. We apply this criterion to nontrivial examples.

This paper is organized as follows: after some preliminaries and fixing some notations, well-posedness and equivalence with a first-order symmetric hyperbolic system gathered in Section 2, we present the main results of exact controllability of System (1) in high frequency (weak observability) in Section 3. Section 4 is devoted to the unique continuation issue for System (1). Appendix 5 contains the proof of some technical lemmas used in the previous sections.

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we recall some results about well-posedness which can be proved exactly as in the scalar case. For the proof of these results in the scalar case, we refer for instance to [27] and the references therein.

φ∣x=0,1=0,in(0,T).\varphi_{\mid x=0,1}=0,~\mathrm{in}~\left(0,T\right).

To summarize, let us introduce the space:

H={(f,g)∈L2(0,1)2×L2(0,1)2,∫01(f−g)=0}.H=\left\{\left(f,g\right)\in L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{2}\times L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{2},~\int_{0}^{1}\left(f-g\right)=0\right\}. (15)

This is clearly a closed subspace of L2​(0,1)2×L2​(0,1)2L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{2}\times L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{2}and thus a Hilbert space with the usual norm (and scalar product) of L2​(0,1)2×L2​(0,1)2.L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{2}\times L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{2}. In view of the previous considerations, we have:

Proposition 3

Let T>0T>0 and HH defined in (15).

  1. 1.

    For any (pT,qT)∈H,\left(p_{T},q_{T}\right)\in H, there exists a unique weak solution (p,q)\left(p,q\right) to (12) such that (p,q)∈C⁡([0,T],H).\left(p,q\right)\in C\left(\left[0,T\right],H\right). Moreover (p−q)∣x=0,1∈L2(0,T)2\left(p-q\right)_{\mid x=0,1}\in L^{2}\left(0,T\right)^{2} and there exists a constant C=C⁡(T,α1,α2)>0C=C\left(T,\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\right)>0 such that:

    ‖(p,q)‖C⁡([0,T],H)+‖(p−q)∣x=0,1‖L2​(0,T)2≤C‖(pT,qT)‖H.\left\|\left(p,q\right)\right\|_{C\left(\left[0,T\right],H\right)}+\left\|\left(p-q\right)_{\mid x=0,1}\right\|_{L^{2}\left(0,T\right)^{2}}\leq C\left\|(p_{T},q_{T})\right\|_{H}.
  2. 2.

    The observability inequality (6) is equivalent to

    ‖(pT,qT)‖H2≤CT​∫0T|B∗​p​(t,0)|2​𝑑t.\left\|(p_{T},q_{T})\right\|_{H}^{2}\leq C_{T}\int_{0}^{T}\left|B^{\ast}p\left(t,0\right)\right|^{2}dt. (16)

We will need in an essential way the block diagonal system associated with System (12):

{pt+px+M∗α1p=0, inQT, qt−qx+M∗α2q=0, inQT, (p+q)∣x=0,1=0ℝ2,in(0,T), (p,q)|t=T=(pT,qT), in(0,1). \left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}p_{t}+p_{x}+M^{\ast}\alpha_{1}p=0,\text{\ }&\mathrm{in}&Q_{T},\text{ \ \ }\\ q_{t}-q_{x}+M^{\ast}\alpha_{2}q=0,\text{ }&\mathrm{in}&Q_{T},\text{ \ \ }\\ (p+q)_{\mid x=0,1}=0_{\mathbb{R}^{2}},&\mathrm{in}&(0,T),\text{ }\\ \left(p,q\right)_{|t=T}=(p_{T},q_{T}),\text{ \ \ }&\mathrm{in}&(0,1).\text{ \ }\end{array}\right. (17)

System (12) is a perturbation of System (17) by the multiplication operator defined on HH by:

𝒫⁡(pq)=(02×2α2​I2×2α1​I2×202×2)​(pq).\mathcal{P}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}p\\ q\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0_{2\times 2}&\alpha_{2}I_{2\times 2}\\ \alpha_{1}I_{2\times 2}&0_{2\times 2}\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}p\\ q\end{array}\right). (18)

The plan now is the following:

  1. 1.

    In a first step (Section 3), we will give necessary and sufficient condition for the solution to the diagonal system (17) to satisfy the observability inequality (16).

  2. 2.

    In a second step and in the same section (Subsection 3.5), and in the same spirit of [21], we will prove that if the solutions of (17) satisfy (16), then up to a finite dimensional subspace of initial data in H,H, the same is true for solutions to System (12). More precisely, we will prove that there exists a compact operator N:H→L2​(0,T),N:H\rightarrow L^{2}(0,T), such that the following weak observability inequality

    ‖(pT,qT)‖H2≤CT​∫0T|B∗​p​(t,0)|2​𝑑t+‖N⁡(pT,qT)‖L2​(0,T)2,\left\|(p_{T},q_{T})\right\|_{H}^{2}\leq C_{T}\int_{0}^{T}\left|B^{\ast}p\left(t,0\right)\right|^{2}dt+\left\|N(p_{T},q_{T})\right\|_{L^{2}(0,T)}^{2}, (19)

    holds. Actually, we will see that N:=p⁡(t,0)−pd​(t,0)N:=p(t,0)-p_{d}(t,0) where pp and pdp_{d} are the solutions of Systems (12) and (17) respectively. Note that by the weak observability inequality entails exact controllability up to finite dimensional space of target states (which are known as the invisible states). More precisely, the observability inequality (16) holds in the orthogonal in HH of the operator (pT,qT)↦p⁡(t,0)(p_{T},q_{T})\mapsto p(t,0) which is finite co-dimensional space. (See [24, Lemma 3]).

  3. 3.

    The last step (Section 4) will provide sufficient (and necessary in some cases) for the unique continuation property to be satisfied (or the Fattorini criterion) for some particular matrix MM and functions α1\alpha_{1} and α2.\alpha_{2}. Nontrivial examples will be developed at the end the section.

3 Weak observability

In the block diagonal system (17), the change of variables t⇌T−tt\rightleftharpoons T-t (we keep the same notations) leads to a system of the from

3.1 Main results

As pointed out above, observability inequality for System (12) will hold modulo compact operator. A classical functional analysis result shows that the space of invisible target is finite codimension and it might be reduced to zero if approximate controllability (or the unique continuation property) holds (See Section 4).

We start by a negative controllability result:

Theorem 4

If T<4,T<4, the weak observability inequality (19) doesn’t hold. More precisely, there is an infinite dimensional space of unreachable target states.

For the proof see Proposition 15 and Remark 16.

Now, we present a positive controllability results. Denote by λ1,λ2\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2} the eigenvalues of M∗M^{\ast} if it is diagonalizable and by μ\mu the multiple eigenvalue of M∗M^{\ast} if it is not. We have the following controllability result:

The proof is rather long, it relies on studying the exact controllability of the diagonal block system (20) combined with a compactness argument. See Propositions 21 and 22 and Remark 23.

Let us make several observations:

Remark 6

To illustrate geometrically the assertions of the above Theorem, we recall that from each point (0,x)\left(0,x\right) (with x∈[0,1]x\in\left[0,1\right]) come two characteristics which stop at some point of the line t=T.t=T. If for example 2​n≤T<2​n+12n\leq T<2n+1 with n≥2,n\geq 2, these characteristics touch the observability boundary [0,T]×{0}\left[0,T\right]\times\left\{0\right\} at least two times at points of the form (2​k−x,0)\left(2k-x,0\right) for one of them and of the form (2​l+x,0)\left(2l+x,0\right) for the other. The conditions on ϕ\phi means that there exist at least two consecutive points of the form (2​k−x,0)\left(2k-x,0\right) and two consecutive points of the form (2​l+x,0)\left(2l+x,0\right) such that the line integrals of the vector field 𝐅=(η1+η22,η1−η22),\boldsymbol{F}=\left(\frac{\eta_{1}+\eta_{2}}{2},\frac{\eta_{1}-\eta_{2}}{2}\right), namely ∫Γ(2​ℓ+x,0)(2​(ℓ+1)+x,0)F⋅γ\int_{\Gamma_{\left(2\ell+x,0\right)}^{\left(2\left(\ell+1\right)+x,0\right)}}F\cdot\gamma and ∫Γ(2​k−x,0)(2​(k+1)−x,0)F⋅γ,\int_{\Gamma_{\left(2k-x,0\right)}^{\left(2\left(k+1\right)-x,0\right)}}F\cdot\gamma, are not, depending on the coupling matrix nature, zero or are not in some discrete set.

Remark 7

Let us first recall that for any t≥2,t\geq 2, the function ϕ\phi defined in (24) is given by

ϕ⁡(t)=∫t−2t−1η1​(τ,τ−(t−2))​𝑑τ+∫t−1tη2​(τ,t−τ)​𝑑τ.\phi\left(t\right)=\int_{t-2}^{t-1}\eta_{1}(\tau,\tau-\left(t-2\right))d\tau+\int_{t-1}^{t}\eta_{2}(\tau,t-\tau)d\tau.

Then, by (21) and (14) we get

ϕ⁡(t)=12​∫01(a+b)​(T−τ+t−2,τ)​𝑑τ+12​∫01(a−b)​(T−t+τ,τ)​𝑑τ.\phi\left(t\right)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\left(a+b\right)\left(T-\tau+t-2,\tau\right)d\tau+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\left(a-b\right)(T-t+\tau,\tau)d\tau.

Observe that in the autonomous case (aa and bb are time independent) the above formulas becomes

ϕ⁡(t)=∫01a⁡(s)​𝑑s.\phi\left(t\right)=\int_{0}^{1}a(s)ds. (27)

Hence, the coupling with first-order derivative in space doesn’t have any influence on the controllability of System (20) in high frequency unless bb depends on time. More precisely, if we let a=0a=0 and b=b⁡(x),b=b(x), then the weak observability inequality (19) doesn’t hold in any time and for any bb since ϕ\phi will be zero. The situation is not the same for parabolic systems. In [17], boundary controllability of a cascade system of two parabolic equations in 1−D1-D has been studied with coupling acting on first-order component. It has been shown that the underlying system is exactly controllable if the coupling function satisfies a moment assumption for the low frequency part and an average assumption like (27) for the high frequency. This shows that differences between hyperbolic and parabolic systems are not limited to the geometric control condition introduced in [10] or the minimal time of control.

Given (t,x)∈QT(t,x)\in Q_{T}, the value of p⁡(t,x)p(t,x) and q⁡(t,x)q(t,x) is determined either by (ps,qs)\left(p_{s},q_{s}\right) or by their values at x=0x=0 or x=1x=1. More precisely, we have by the characteristics method:

p⁡(t,x)={exp⁡(M∗​∫t−xtη1​(τ,τ−(t−x))​dτ)​p​(t−x,0),ift−x>s,exp⁡(M∗​∫stη1​(τ,τ−(t−x))​dτ)​ps​(x−t+s),ift−x<s,p(t,x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\exp\left(M^{\ast}\int_{t-x}^{t}\eta_{1}(\tau,\tau-(t-x))d\tau\right)p(t-x,0),&\mathrm{if}&t-x>s,\\ &&\\ \exp\left(M^{\ast}\int_{s}^{t}\eta_{1}(\tau,\tau-(t-x))d\tau\right)p_{s}(x-t+s),&\mathrm{if}&t-x<s,\end{array}\right. (28)

and

q⁡(t,x)={exp⁡(M∗​∫x+t−1tη2​(τ,t+x−τ)​dτ)​q​(t+x−1,1),ift+x−1>s,exp⁡(M∗​∫stη2​(τ,t+x−τ)​dτ)​qs​(x+t−s),ift+x−1<s.q(t,x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\exp\left(M^{\ast}\int_{x+t-1}^{t}\eta_{2}(\tau,t+x-\tau)d\tau\right)q(t+x-1,1),&\mathrm{if}&t+x-1>s,\\ &&\\ \exp\left(M^{\ast}\int_{s}^{t}\eta_{2}(\tau,t+x-\tau)d\tau\right)q_{s}(x+t-s),&\mathrm{if}&t+x-1<s.\end{array}\right. (29)

Thus, computing p⁡(t,x)p(t,x) and q⁡(t,x)q(t,x) amounts to evaluate p⁡(t,0)p(t,0) and q⁡(t,1)q(t,1) (respectively) as functions of the initial data (p0,q0)(p_{0},q_{0}), keeping in mind the boundary conditions. The following lemma can be proved by induction:

Lemma 8

Let n≥0n\geq 0 be an integer and Zs=(ps,qs)∈H.Z_{s}=(p_{s},q_{s})\in H. Then if Z=(p,q)Z=(p,q) is the solution to System (22), one has:

p(t,0)=−efn​(t,s)​M∗qs(t−s−2n), if 2n≤t−s<2n+1,p(t,0)=-e^{f_{n}(t,s)M^{\ast}}q_{s}(t-s-2n),\text{ }\mathrm{if}\text{ }2n\leq t-s<2n+1, (30)

3.3 Some technical results on multiplication operators

In order to make clear the proof of our exact observability results, we will need some preliminary results on multiplications operators defined from L2​(0,1)kL^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{k} in L2​(0,1)nL^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{n} for some positive integers k,n.k,n.

Let M=(mi​j)1≤i,j≤nM=\left(m_{ij}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq n} a n×nn\times n matrix whose entries satisfies mi​j∈C⁡([0,1],ℝ).m_{ij}\in C\left(\left[0,1\right],\mathbb{R}\right). The multiplication operator 𝕄:L2​(0,1)k\mathbb{M}:L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{k} →L2​(0,1)n\rightarrow L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{n} associated with MM is defined by:

(𝕄​h)​(x)=M⁡(x)​h​(x),x∈(0,1),h∈L2​(0,1)n.\left(\mathbb{M}h\right)\left(x\right)=M\left(x\right)h(x),~x\in\left(0,1\right),~h\in L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{n}.

Clearly 𝕄\mathbb{M} is a bounded operator. When s=n,s=n, the following characterization of the invertibility of 𝕄\mathbb{M} is derived from [19, Proposition 2.2]:

Proposition 10

The operator 𝕄:L2​(0,1)k\mathbb{M}:L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{k} →L2​(0,1)k\rightarrow L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{k} is invertible if, and only if:

infx∈[0,1]|detM⁡(x)|>0.\inf_{x\in\left[0,1\right]}\left|\det M\left(x\right)\right|>0.

We are now interested by the case k<nk<n .

Proposition 11

Let k<nk<n and 𝕄:L2​(0,1)k\mathbb{M}:L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{k} →L2​(0,1)n.\rightarrow L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{n}. The following properties are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    There exists a constant C>0C>0 such that

    ‖h‖L2​(0,1)k≤C​‖𝕄​h‖L2​(0,1)n,∀h∈L2​(0,1)k.\left\|h\right\|_{L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{k}}\leq C\left\|\mathbb{M}h\right\|_{L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{n}},~\forall h\in L^{2}\left(0,1\right)^{k}.
  2. 2.

    For all x∈[0,1],x\in\left[0,1\right], there exists a s×ss\times s matrix MextM_{\mathrm{ext}}, extracted from M,M,~such that

    detMext​(x)≠0.\det M_{\mathrm{ext}}\left(x\right)\neq 0.

Proof. For the proof, see Appendix 5.

Remark 16

The above proposition shows that if T<4T<4 then the diagonal system (20) is not exactly controllable. Combining this and the fact that the difference of the input maps is compact (See Theorem 24) entails that System (12) is not weakly controllable; more precisely, there exists an infinite dimensional space of unreachable target states.

It has to be pointed out that the previous negative observability result does not depend of the choice of η1,η2\eta_{1},\eta_{2} and M.M.

Before going one in the analysis, let us give a necessary condition for the exact observability to hold:

Remark 23

Up to now, we have dealt only with the block diagonal system (22), and by Propositions 21 and 22, we have obtained a necessary and sufficient conditions that guarantee the exact controllability of System (22). In the next subsection, we will prove a compactness result which will allow to extend the obtained results to the complete system (12) up to finite dimensional space of target states. Indeed, we have proved that there exists a CT>0C_{T}>0 such that

‖(p0,q0)‖H2≤CT​∫0T|B∗​pd​(t,0)|2​𝑑t,\left\|(p_{0},q_{0})\right\|_{H}^{2}\leq C_{T}\int_{0}^{T}\left|B^{\ast}p_{d}\left(t,0\right)\right|^{2}dt,

where (pd,qd)\left(p_{d},q_{d}\right) is the solution of the diagonal system (22). Now, by using the triangular inequality we obtain

‖(p0,q0)‖H2≤CT​∫0T|B∗​p​(t,0)|2​𝑑t+CT​∫0T|B∗​(p−pd)​(t,0)|2​𝑑t,\left\|(p_{0},q_{0})\right\|_{H}^{2}\leq C_{T}\int_{0}^{T}\left|B^{\ast}p\left(t,0\right)\right|^{2}dt+C_{T}\int_{0}^{T}\left|B^{\ast}\left(p-p_{d}\right)\left(t,0\right)\right|^{2}dt,

where (p,q)\left(p,q\right) is the solution of the complete system (12). So, if we can prove that the map (p0,q0)t↦B∗(p−pd)∣x=0(p_{0},q_{0})^{t}\mapsto B^{\ast}\left(p-p_{d}\right)_{\mid x=0} is compact, we can then conclude that the complete system (12) is exactly controllable for any target state in the orthogonal in HH of the operator (p0,q0)t↦B∗​p​(t,0)(p_{0},q_{0})^{t}\mapsto B^{\ast}p(t,0) (see for instance [24, Lemma 3]). Notice that if its kernel is reduced to zero then exact controllability holds for the complete system (12).

3.5 Compactness

In section 3, we have, after the change of variable t⇌T−t,t\rightleftharpoons T-t, considered the System (20) that we recall here:

{pt+px−M∗​η1​p=0,inQT, qt−qx−M∗η2q=0, inQT, (p+q)∣x=0,1=0ℝ2,in(0,T), (p,q)|t=0=(p0,q0), in(0,1). \left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}p_{t}+p_{x}-M^{\ast}\eta_{1}p=0,&\mathrm{in}&Q_{T},\text{ \ \ }\\ q_{t}-q_{x}-M^{\ast}\eta_{2}q=0,\text{\ }&\mathrm{in}&Q_{T},\text{ \ \ }\\ (p+q)_{\mid x=0,1}=0_{\mathbb{R}^{2}},&\mathrm{in}&(0,T),\text{ }\\ \left(p,q\right)_{|t=0}=(p_{0},q_{0}),\text{\ \ \ \ }&\mathrm{in}&(0,1).\text{ \ }\end{array}\right. (58)

In the sequel, we denote by Z=Z⁡(t,⋅,s,p0,q0)=(p,q)​(t,⋅,s,p0,q0)Z=Z\left(t,\cdot,s;p_{0},q_{0}\right)=\left(p,q\right)\left(t,\cdot,s;p_{0},q_{0}\right) the solution to (58) and by Zd=Zd​(t,⋅,s,p0,q0)=(pd,qd)​(t,⋅,s,p0,q0)Z_{d}=Z_{d}\left(t,\cdot;s,p_{0},q_{0}\right)=\left(p_{d},q_{d}\right)\left(t,\cdot,s;p_{0},q_{0}\right) the solution to the diagonal system (59).

DT:H→L2​(0,T)(p0,q0)t↦B∗(p−pd)∣x=0.\begin{array}[]{cccc}D_{T}:&H&\rightarrow&L^{2}\left(0,T\right)\\ &(p_{0},q_{0})^{t}&\mapsto&B^{\ast}\left(p-p_{d}\right)_{\mid x=0}.\end{array}

Theorem 24

Let T>0T>0. Then the operator DTD_{T} is compact.

+∫0tUd(t,s)𝒫T(s)Ud(s,0)Z0ds.\displaystyle+\int_{0}^{t}U_{d}(t,s)\mathcal{P}_{T}(s)U_{d}(s,0)Z_{0}ds.

4 Unique continuation

In this section, we deal with the unique continuation property for System (1). We give a necessary and sufficient condition for the constant case, and a semi-explicit condition in the autonomous case. When the coefficients depend on time, we give also a necessary and sufficient condition for the cascade case with providing some non-trivial examples at the end.

4.1 The constant case

Here, we assume that a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R}. Recall that the adjoint system of System (1) is given by

{φt​t=φx​x−M∗​(a​φt+b​φx),in(0,T)×(0,1),φ∣x=0,1=0, in(0,T), (φ,φt)∣t=T=(φT0,φT1), in(0,1). \left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\varphi_{tt}=\varphi_{xx}-M^{\ast}(a\varphi_{t}+b\varphi_{x}),&\mathrm{in}&(0,T)\times(0,1),\\ \varphi_{\mid x=0,1}=0,\text{ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ }&\mathrm{in}&(0,T),\text{ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ }\\ \left(\varphi,\varphi_{t}\right)_{\mid t=T}=\left(\varphi^{T}_{0},\varphi^{T}_{1}\right),\text{ \ \ }&\mathrm{in}&(0,1).\text{ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ }\end{array}\right. For the sake of simplicity, we set eb​x2​M∗​φ~​(x)=φ⁡(x).e^{\frac{bx}{2}M^{\ast}}\widetilde{\varphi}(x)=\varphi(x). Then φ~\widetilde{\varphi} is the solution of the following system

{φ~t​t=φ~x​x−14​b2​(M∗)2​φ~−a​M∗​φ~t,in(0,T)×(0,1),φ~∣x=0,1=0, in(0,T), (φ~,φ~t)∣t=T=(φ~T0,φ~T1), in(0,1). \left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}\widetilde{\varphi}_{tt}=\widetilde{\varphi}_{xx}-\frac{1}{4}b^{2}\left(M^{\ast}\right)^{2}\widetilde{\varphi}-aM^{\ast}\widetilde{\varphi}_{t},&\mathrm{in}&(0,T)\times(0,1),\\ \widetilde{\varphi}_{\mid x=0,1}=0,\text{ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ }&\mathrm{in}&(0,T),\text{ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ }\\ \left(\widetilde{\varphi},\widetilde{\varphi}_{t}\right)_{\mid t=T}=\left(\widetilde{\varphi}^{T}_{0},\widetilde{\varphi}^{T}_{1}\right),\text{ \ \ }&\mathrm{in}&(0,1).\text{ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ }\end{array}\right.

As it is shown, if we let a=0a=0, the coupling parameter bb affects controllability in low frequency. Actually, conditions (90) and (91) become respectively

4.2 The authonomous case

When the coefficients don’t depend on time, we can give a characterization to cover the invisible target states by applying the Fattorini criterion on system (12) which is possible since the difference between the control maps is compact by Theroem 24 (See [16, Remarks 2.4 and 1.5]). Note that the Fattorini criterion with the fact that the two control maps is compact implies exact controllability of the complete system (12) in the same minimal time T=4T=4. So, in order to cover the invisible target states we have to ensure that

ker(sI−𝒜∗)∩ker(C∗)={0}, ∀s∈ℂ,\ker(sI-\mathcal{A}^{\ast})\cap\ker(C^{\ast})=\{0\},\text{ }\forall s\in\mathbb{C}, (92)

and let Rs​(⋅,⋅)R_{s}(\cdot,\cdot) the fundamental matrix of the finite dimensional system

In this subsection we prove the unique continuation property for a particular class of System (20). We assume in the sequel that the matrix MM and the vector BB have the following form:

for any (p0−,p0+,q0−,q0+)∈\left(p_{0}^{-},p_{0}^{+},q_{0}^{-},q_{0}^{+}\right)\in D⁡(𝒜∗)D(\mathcal{A}^{\ast}) where D⁡(𝒜∗)D(\mathcal{A}^{\ast}) is defined in (93).

Observe that the first and the third equations of the above system are free. The idea is to solve these equations explicitly and then considering their solution as a second member for the second and the fourth equations. Let us start by solving the homogeneous part of System (98). i.e.

{pt−+px−=0,inQT,qt−−qx−=0,inQT,(p++q+)|x=0,1=0,in(0,T),(p−,q−)|t=0=(p0−,q0−),in(0,1).\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}p_{t}^{-}+p_{x}^{-}=0,&\mathrm{in}&Q_{T},\\ q_{t}^{-}-q_{x}^{-}=0,&\mathrm{in}&Q_{T},\\ \left(p^{+}+q^{+}\right)_{|x=0,1}=0,&\mathrm{in}&(0,T),\\ \left(p^{-},q^{-}\right)_{|t=0}=\left(p_{0}^{-},q_{0}^{-}\right),&\mathrm{in}&(0,1).\end{array}\right. Lemma 34

The solution (p−,q−)(p^{-},q^{-}) to System (99) are given by

p−​(t,x)={p0−​(x−t+2​n),if2​n−1≤t−x≤2​n,−q0−(t−x−2n), if2​n≤t−x≤2​n+1,​n≥0,p^{-}(t,x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}p_{0}^{-}(x-t+2n),&\mathrm{if}&2n-1\leq t-x\leq 2n,\\ -q_{0}^{-}(t-x-2n),\text{ \ }&\mathrm{if}&2n\leq t-x\leq 2n+1,\end{array}\right.n\geq 0, (100)

{pt++px+=f, inQT,qt+−qx+=f,inQT,(p++q+)|x=1=p|x=0+=0,in(0,T),(p+,q+)|t=0=(p0+,q0+).in(0,1).\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}p_{t}^{+}+p_{x}^{+}=f,\text{ }&\mathrm{in}&Q_{T},\\ q_{t}^{+}-q_{x}^{+}=f,&\mathrm{in}&Q_{T},\\ \left(p^{+}+q^{+}\right)_{|x=1}=p_{|x=0}^{+}=0,&\mathrm{in}&(0,T),\\ \left(p^{+},q^{+}\right)_{|t=0}=\left(p_{0}^{+},q_{0}^{+}\right).&\mathrm{in}&(0,1).\end{array}\right. Theorem 37

Let n≥2n\geq 2 be an integer. The unique continuation property for (98) holds true at time TT if, and only if, there exist k,l≥1k,l\geq 1 such that the unique solution (p0−,q0−)\left(p_{0}^{-},q_{0}^{-}\right) to Equation (148) is the null one.

    2. 2.

which are a second kind Fredholm integral equations. The following corollary is a straightforward consequence of the above theorem:

Corollary 38

Let n≥2n\geq 2 be an integer. Assume that (149) and (152) hold for some k,l≥1k,l\geq 1. The unique continuation property for (98) holds at time TT if, and only if 1∉σ⁡(𝒦k,l).1\notin\sigma\left(\mathcal{K}_{k,l}\right).

Proof. By assumptions (149)-(152), the Equation (148) is Fredholm integral equation of second kind. By the Fredholm alternative, it possesses a unique solution if, and only if 1∉σ⁡(𝒦k,l),1\notin\sigma\left(\mathcal{K}_{k,l}\right), for some l,k≥1.l,k\geq 1.  

Remark 39

Since the component of the kernel Ak,l−1​(⋅)​𝕂n,k,l​(⋅,⋅),A_{k,l}^{-1}(\cdot)\mathbb{K}_{n,k,l}(\cdot,\cdot), n≥k,l≥1,n\geq k,l\geq 1, are completely known, we can always prove that 1∉σ⁡(𝒦k,l),1\notin\sigma\left(\mathcal{K}_{k,l}\right), by assuming that ‖𝒦k,l‖ℒ⁡(L2​(0,1,M2×2​(ℝ)))\left\|\mathcal{K}_{k,l}\right\|_{\mathcal{L}\left(L^{2}(0,1;M_{2\times 2}(\mathbb{R}))\right)} <1.<1. Notice that this is not necessarily a smallness assumption on the coupling coefficients since the kernel involves the matrix Ak,l−1​(⋅)A_{k,l}^{-1}(\cdot).

Remark 40

It is not difficult to see that if η1\eta_{1} and η2\eta_{2} are time independent, the compact operator 𝒦k,l=𝒦,\mathcal{K}_{k,l}=\mathcal{K}, is symmetric. Therefore, its spectrum consists of real eigenvalues. However, giving a characterization of the spectrum needs more care.

Remark 41

In [11], it has been shown that the unique continuation property for a⁡(t,x)=a⁡(x)a(t,x)=a(x) and b=0b=0 holds at time T>0T>0 for System (98) if, and only if T≥4,T\geq 4, and

∫01a(s)sin2(πns)ds≠0, ∀n≥1.\int_{0}^{1}a(s)\sin^{2}(\pi ns)ds\neq 0,\text{ }\forall n\geq 1. (154)

It is natural to expect that condition (154) is equivalent to the uniqueness of the solution to Equation (148) for 𝕂n,k,l=𝕂\mathbb{K}_{n,k,l}=\mathbb{K}.

Remark 42

With a simple change of variable (see [4, Remark 15]), we can deduce that all the results proved for cascade system with velocity coupling (a≠0a\neq 0) hold true for zero order coupling (replace a​φta\varphi_{t} by a​φa\varphi in System (3)) in the space
